source.version_note: Filosofia Unisinos / Unisinos Journal of Philosophy 25(1):e25111 (2024). Submitted 16 November 2023, accepted 13 January 2024.
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read, including Portuguese abstract, quotations, footnotes and bibliography. Separate publisher metadata and SEP archive checked only for two reference corrections, not full reading of those works.

citation.title: The heart of an AI: agency, moral sense, and friendship

reading.source_scope_note: Philosophical analysis grounded in moral sentimentalism and accounts of friendship. No original experiment, longitudinal chatbot-user sample, machine-emotion test or clinical intervention evaluation.
access_limits: All 16 supplied pages read, including quoted passages from books. The underlying complete books, cited primary psychology studies and chatbot products were not independently read, reproduced or tested.

Friendship archive author/title and Pentina article authors were checked separately. These limited metadata checks do not supply full-text evidence of chatbot effects or imply the original cited studies were read.

study.type: Conceptual philosophical argument, not an original empirical study or systematic review.
study.premise: An explicitly adopted emotional-lapse assumption holds that lack of moral feelings impairs full moral agency. The argument uses Hume/Smith sentimentalism, theories of agency and philosophical friendship components.
study.relationship_account: Mutual care, trust/intimacy, shared experiences and mutual liking are contrasted with claimed asymmetry of commercial chatbot companionship. Social displacement, echo chambers and diminished conflict skills are proposed risks rather than newly measured outcomes.
study.evidence_gap: The paragraph claiming a study of prolonged Replika use literally contains '(cite research)'; the Aristotle discussion contains '(cite works)'. The bibliography includes Pentina's Replika article, but the placeholder is not resolved to a specific measured harmful outcome.

summary: Add self-disclosing trust as a relational concept, enrich sympathy and emotional-dependency discussions with explicit conceptual scope, and record unresolved causal claims and verified source-identity corrections. Do not turn the author's emotional-lapse premise into a proven AI diagnosis or a universal impossibility theorem.

findings.definition: Trust that another person will reliably understand one's personal concerns and intentions, enabling mutual intimate disclosure.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary relational concept in a fully read philosophical article; no direct measurement or causal test in human–AI use
findings.ai_proposal: Investigate whether people disclose personal matters to an AI because they expect consistent understanding, while separately measuring actual comprehension, privacy expectations and data handling. Explain the system's role and limits without implying reciprocal human intimacy or encouraging unnecessary sensitive disclosure.
findings.novelty_rationale: A particular relational expectation supporting intimate disclosure, distinct from generic confidence in task competence, the act of disclosure itself, a reciprocity norm, betrayal aversion or dependency. The name and account are explicitly present rather than invented as a new AI syndrome.

evidence.quote: At the core of self-disclosing trust lies the question of whether a person can trust another to comprehend personal matters, and to do so consistently.

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion attributes mutual self-disclosing trust to Thomas's account of friendship, then connects consistent understanding to vulnerability and intimacy. It is a philosophical definition, not a validated chatbot scale or an observed disclosure effect. Thomas's full original chapter remains unread.
findings.boundary: Trust is not proof of accurate understanding, confidentiality, secure storage, beneficial advice or reciprocal feeling. Disclosure may be appropriate without friendship, and a person can value AI support without mistaking it for a human relationship. No machine subjective intimacy or need is inferred.

findings.term: Sympathy in moral sentimentalism and friendship
findings.definition: Concern for another's welfare is treated as important to moral judgment and mutual care in the article's sentimentalist account.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing sympathy entry receives a second fully read conceptual source. Do not create an emotional-lapse behavior from an assumed absence of this feeling or merge sympathy with every form of empathy.

findings.evidence_scope: A philosophical account of moral feeling and friendship, with secondary discussion of Smith, Hume and Annis. The authors explicitly use sympathy as a methodological umbrella even where originals say empathy. No direct feeling, human behavioral mechanism or absence of machine consciousness is experimentally established.
findings.boundary: Concern, emotional contagion, perspective taking and shared feeling need not be the same process. The article's broad terminology is not adopted as a general synonym rule. Sentimentalism's role for emotion is a philosophical position, not proof that feeling guarantees ethical conduct or that functional ethical behavior requires subjective human emotion.

findings.term: Companionship displacement and one-sided relational expectations
findings.definition: Habitual one-sided AI companionship is proposed to displace human contact or shape expectations of relationships around one's own preferences.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing dependency/displacement concern covers this proposed pattern; no separate chatbot-friendship decay syndrome is introduced.

findings.evidence_scope: The article reasons conditionally from a philosophical asymmetry in chatbot friendship to possible social displacement and reduced reciprocal expectations. It supplies no new longitudinal data; a claimed Replika study contains an unresolved citation placeholder. This is relevant conceptual risk evidence, not an established causal effect or prevalence estimate.
findings.boundary: Frequent or valued AI use does not by itself establish harmful dependency, isolation, abusive behavior or lost social skills. Displacement must be measured against human-support opportunities, prior isolation and benefits. The paper acknowledges potential support benefits but does not quantify either benefits or harms.

methodological_limits: The emotional-lapse assumption is introduced as a premise rooted in moral sentimentalism. No sample, measurement, intervention or formal proof establishes that every AI lacks all moral understanding or that an emotional capacity is necessary/sufficient for every justified ethical action.

Claims that full moral agency is impossible, that models only follow initial rules or that AGI necessarily reaches a singularity are philosophical or speculative generalizations. Practical ethical performance, subjective experience, moral status and legal accountability must be separated.

The I, Robot rescue and paperclip maximizer are illustrative fictional/thought-experiment cases, not empirical evaluations of AI. Numerical survival rates and the later inconsistent character name are not verified real-world outcomes.

The article's categorical genetic-predestination explanation is not established by the cited summaries. Genetic influence is not behavioral inevitability, nor proof that teaching concern is irrelevant.

Autism, psychopathy and Williams syndrome are grouped under broad sympathy claims without original assessment here. These summaries must not be used to infer an individual person's emotions, moral worth, clinical diagnosis or decision rights. Sympathy, empathy components and cognitive abilities are not interchangeable.

The source explicitly substitutes sympathy for empathy in some primary accounts. That terminology choice can blur motor mimicry, emotional contagion, concern, perspective taking and targeted helping; it is not a validated equivalence.

No experiment shows that machine emotion-recognition outputs reveal subjective understanding, or that generic chatbots can all sense facial expressions, body language and voice. Capabilities depend on modalities, implementation and validation.

Moral feelings do not guarantee justified judgment, and lack of demonstrated feelings does not by itself establish every generated decision is wrong. Distinguish functional performance from the philosophical requirements of full moral agency.

The claimed prolonged-use Replika research contains '(cite research)'; another passage contains '(cite works)'. These are unresolved support gaps, not quotations from an identified verified primary experiment.

Companion marketing, news, philosophical accounts, robot descriptions and anecdotes have different evidential roles. The claim to maintain mental health is promotional text, not clinical evidence. No treatment recommendation or clinical efficacy is inferred.

A one-sided relationship may be meaningful or helpful to a person without being reciprocal human friendship. The argument does not measure whether AI supplements or displaces human contact, nor establish that every user mistakes simulation for reciprocal feeling.

Causal claims about declining social skills, controlling behavior, abuse, isolation or friendship quality require comparison groups and longitudinal measures. Pre-existing loneliness and selection into chatbot use can produce similar associations.

The discussion of hikikomori and Korean isolation relies on news-level population summaries and philosophical inference. It does not diagnose users, establish uniform causes or demonstrate a chatbot intervention worsens seclusion.

The claim most listed systems sell a perfect virtual girlfriend collapses organizations, general chat platforms and specialized companion products. Their actual features, pricing, initiative and safety practices were not tested; present-day behavior must not be inferred from 2023 descriptions.

The source's no-self-interest condition for shared activity is stronger than ordinary accounts requiring friendship to be at least part of the motivation. Mixed motives do not automatically make human friendship inauthentic.

Reference gaps and mismatches include incorrect Helm identity, missing Pentina coauthors, an unrelated Bian interface citation, Gert/Kauppinen year differences and an incomplete Wallach/Allen year. Only independently checked corrections above are presented as reliable replacements.
Quoted excerpts from Smith, Hume, Aristotle, Nozick and friendship chapters are not equivalent to reading their complete books. Their theories are not counted as separate fully read research papers.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The earlier moral-agency research and this philosophical account both require separating perceived sympathy, felt sympathy, moral performance and attributed responsibility. The current argument is not another direct experimental replication.
Perceived experience in a described robot differs from actual conscious feeling. An attributed mind or supportive response cannot settle the emotional-lapse premise.

An explicitly supportive persona permits constructive disagreement, so a claim all chatbots only mirror users is too broad. Prompt design can change observed style without establishing reciprocal feeling or long-term social benefit.

deferred.reason: Author-labeled sentimentalist premise about missing emotion, not a measured independent behavior or established universal impossibility result. Its relation to sympathy and relational asymmetry is documented without creating an AI diagnosis.

The paper quotes Smith on the spectator evaluating one's conduct but does not explicitly define the impartial-spectator construct as such. Avoid adding the broader canonical label from outside assumptions; full primary work remains unread.
Overlaps existing dependency/displacement concern; causal effects and the alleged supporting study are not adequately identified here.

limitations: One new relational concept and two existing conceptual evidence notes; no automatic harm edges, clinical claims or independent empirical confirmations are manufactured.
